The other day, I found an old journal tucked beneath a pile of books in my attic. The pages were yellowed with time, the ink faded but still legible in spots. The first entry was dated 1987, and it began with a single sentence: *"Today, I learned that the world is bigger than I thought."* The writer, my grandmother, had been twelve years old when she wrote it. She’d just moved to a new town, and the journal was her way of making sense of the chaos—new friends, a strange house, the way the wind sounded different here.

I sat cross-legged on the attic floor, flipping through the pages. Some entries were mundane: *"Mom made spaghetti again. I hate spaghetti."* Others were poetic in their simplicity: *"The river looks like liquid silver at sunset."* There was a drawing of a cat she’d named Whiskers, though I’d never met any such animal. The last entry was from her sixteenth birthday, and it read: *"I don’t know what I want to be when I grow up, but I know I want to keep writing. Even if no one ever reads it."*

I closed the journal, holding it to my chest. It was a small thing, really—a relic of someone else’s life—but it made me think about how we all carry these quiet, unassuming stories. My grandmother never became a famous writer, but she left behind something that mattered. Maybe the point isn’t to be remembered by everyone, but to leave a trace of yourself for the people who stumble upon your words later.

I wonder what I’ll leave behind. A journal? A half-finished novel? A single sentence scribbled on a napkin? For now, I’ll keep writing, even if no one reads it. Because sometimes, the act itself is enough.
